Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. education: Some college or Associate's degree.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. income: Less than $30,000.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Science Above Politics: Former Skeptics' Defense of Climate Science

Jennifer Rukavina

When Jennifer Rukavina became a television meteorologist, she noticed her colleagues were divided into two camps: believers and nonbelievers. Ms. Rukavina didn’t know at first which camp she fell into, but she certainly wasn’t “convinced” about climate change.

In the early 2000s, when Ms. Rukavina began her career, Al Gore, the former vice president and climate change activist, had just released his film “An Inconvenient Truth.” The split among her colleagues, Ms. Rukavina said, was largely focused around the political “theater” surrounding the film, which experts often describe as a flash point in the deepening partisan divide on climate change.

“I decided that I needed to educate myself, because the meteorologist is often viewed as the station scientist,” Ms. Rukavina said. In 2008, she attended her first Glen Gerberg Weather and Climate Summit — a meeting of weathercasters and climate scientists — in Colorado. After hearing from the scientists themselves, Ms. Rukavina said, she changed her mind.

“I am a registered Republican, but I don’t let politics dictate what good science is to me,” she said. Every year since, Ms. Rukavina has briefed her viewers live from the conference. “It really doesn’t matter to me what my viewers think of climate change,” she said. “What matters to me most is being able to prepare them for the changes that lie ahead.”

Bob Inglis

Bob Inglis was a congressman from one of the most conservative districts in South Carolina, one of the reddest states of the nation. The National Rifle Association endorsed him, and so did the American Conservative Union. For his first six years in Congress, he believed that climate change was, in his own words, “a bunch of hooey.”

Then, Inglis had a change of heart: “When I ran again in 2004, my son had just turned 18 and was voting for the first time. He said to me, ‘Dad, I'll vote for you, but you're gonna clean up your act on the environment.’ So, I listened to my family, got in the House Science Committee, got the opportunity to go to Antarctica, and saw the evidence in the ice core drillings—they show that the Earth's atmosphere has changed, and it's the burning of fossil fuels that has changed it, creating stronger storms and the risk of flooding from higher sea levels.”

Inglis sees protecting Earth’s climate as a conservative priority: “A lot of us conservatives would like to avoid the issue [of climate change], because we assume it means drastic changes and a bigger government. It doesn't have to be that way. The conservative thing to do is to protect our families and nation against this threat. We can create a new energy future that has lots of jobs and lots of wealth creation, and that lights up the world with more energy, more mobility, [and] more freedom.”

Trust in climate scientists is strong. In a recent Pew Research Center national survey, 
76%

Though this may seem surprising in our polarized context, Americans share many values and beliefs.

Sources:

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/08/09/why-some-americans-do-not-see-urgency-on-climate-change/

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. education: Less than high school.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Trust in climate scientists is strong. In a recent Pew Research Center national survey, 
76%
 of Americans reported having at least some trust in climate scientists to provide full and accurate information about climate change. Only 23% of Americans said they had little or no trust in climate scientists.

Though this may seem surprising in our polarized context, Americans share many values and beliefs.

Sources:

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/08/09/why-some-americans-do-not-see-urgency-on-climate-change/ 

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/01/15/americans-confidence-in-scientists/

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. education: Some college or Associate's degree.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Trust in climate scientists is strong. In a recent Pew Research Center national survey, 
76%
 of Americans reported having at least some trust in climate scientists to provide full and accurate information about climate change. Only 23% of Americans said they had little or no trust in climate scientists.

Though this may seem surprising in our polarized context, Americans share many values and beliefs.

Sources:

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/08/09/why-some-americans-do-not-see-urgency-on-climate-change/ 

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/01/15/americans-confidence-in-scientists/

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Trust in climate scientists is strong. In a recent Pew Research Center national survey, 
76%
 of Americans reported having at least some trust in climate scientists to provide full and accurate information about climate change. Only 23% of Americans said they had little or no trust in climate scientists.

Though this may seem surprising in our polarized context, Americans share many values and beliefs.

Sources:

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/08/09/why-some-americans-do-not-see-urgency-on-climate-change/ 

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/01/15/americans-confidence-in-scientists/

trust_competence_3: How unqualified or qualified are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very unqualified to 100: very qualified

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. party: Other.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Trust in climate scientists is strong. In a recent Pew Research Center national survey, 
76%
 of Americans reported having at least some trust in climate scientists to provide full and accurate information about climate change. Only 23% of Americans said they had little or no trust in climate scientists.

Though this may seem surprising in our polarized context, Americans share many values and beliefs.

Sources:

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/08/09/why-some-americans-do-not-see-urgency-on-climate-change/ 

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/01/15/americans-confidence-in-scientists/

QUESTION_ID: QUESTION? ANSWER_OPTIONS
trust_competence_1: How incompetent or competent are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very incompetent to 100: very competent
trust_competence_2: How unintelligent or intelligent are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very unintelligent to 100: very intelligent
trust_competence_3: How unqualified or qualified are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very unqualified to 100: very qualified
trust_integrity_1: How dishonest or honest are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very dishonest to 100: very honest
trust_integrity_2: How unethical or ethical are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very unethical to 100: very ethical
trust_integrity_3: How insincere or sincere are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very insincere to 100: very sincere
trust_benevolence_1: How unconcerned or concerned are most climate scientists about people’s wellbeing? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very unconcerned to 100: very concerned
trust_benevolence_2: How uneager or eager are most climate scientists to improve others’ lives? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very uneager to 100: very eager
trust_benevolence_3: How inconsiderate or considerate are most climate scientists of others’ interests? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very inconsiderate to 100: very considerate
trust_openness_1: How open, if at all, are most climate scientists to feedback? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not open at all to 100: Very open
trust_openness_2: How unwilling or willing are most climate scientists to be transparent? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very unwilling to 100: Very willing
trust_openness_3: How much or how little attention do climate scientists pay to other people's views? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very little attention to 100: A great deal of attention
trust_post: How much do you trust climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Very strongly
distrust_post: How much do you distrust climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Very strongly
funding_perceptions: Do you think the federal government is spending too much, too little or about the right amount of money on climate change research? The person answers on a slider from 0: Far too little to 100: Far too much
belief_post: How accurate do you think this statement is? Human activities are causing climate change. The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all accurate to 100: Extremely accurate
policy_general: Should the U.S. government do more to reduce global warming? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
donation_ams: Of the $10 bonus, how much would you like to donate to the American Meteorological Society (AMS)? The person answers on a slider from 0: 0$ to 10: 10$
newsletter_signup: Did you subscribe to the Talking Climate newsletter on the previous page? Options are: 1: Yes, 2: No
inst_trust_epa: How much do you trust the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Very strongly
inst_trust_nasa: How much do you trust the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Very strongly
inst_trust_noaa: How much do you trust the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Very strongly
inst_trust_universities: How much do you trust universities and colleges? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Very strongly
inst_trust_federal_gov: How much do you trust the federal government? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Very strongly
policy_role_1: Climate scientists should work closely with policy makers to integrate scientific results into policy-making. The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly disagree to 100: Strongly agree
policy_role_2: Climate scientists should actively advocate for specific policies. The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly disagree to 100: Strongly agree
policy_role_3: Climate scientists should communicate their findings to policy makers. The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly disagree to 100: Strongly agree
policy_role_4: Climate scientists should be more involved in the policy-making process. The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly disagree to 100: Strongly agree
concern_1: How concerned are you about climate change? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Extremely
concern_2: How serious a problem is climate change? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Extremely
concern_3: Relative to other issues facing the U.S., how important is climate change? The person answers on a slider from 0: The least important issue to 100: The most important issue
policy_specific_1: How much do you support or oppose raising taxes on fossil fuels (e.g., gas, oil, coal)? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
policy_specific_2: How much do you support or oppose expanding infrastructure for public transportation? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
policy_specific_3: How much do you support or oppose increasing the use of sustainable energy such as wind and solar energy? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
policy_specific_4: How much do you support or oppose protecting forested and land areas? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
policy_specific_5: How much do you support or oppose increasing taxes on carbon-intensive foods (e.g. beef and dairy products)? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
policy_specific_6: How much do you support or oppose investing more in green jobs and businesses? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
policy_specific_7: How much do you support or oppose introducing laws to keep waterways and oceans clean? The person answers on a slider from 0: Strongly oppose to 100: Strongly support
behavior_meat: How likely are you to eat less meat in the next twelve months? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not likely at all to 100: Extremely likely
behavior_transport: How likely are you to walk bicycle carpool or take public transportation more often instead of driving by yourself in the next twelve months? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not likely at all to 100: Extremely likely
behavior_solar: How likely are you to install a solar panel in the next twelve months? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not likely at all to 100: Extremely likely
behavior_fly: How likely are you to go on less personal (non-business) air travel in the next twelve months? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not likely at all to 100: Extremely likely
behavior_talk: How likely are you to talk to friends and family about the importance of climate change in the next twelve months? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not likely at all to 100: Extremely likely
behavior_donate: How likely are you to donate to an environmental NGO in the next twelve months? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not likely at all to 100: Extremely likely

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Trust in climate scientists is strong. In a recent Pew Research Center national survey, 
76%
 of Americans reported having at least some trust in climate scientists to provide full and accurate information about climate change. Only 23% of Americans said they had little or no trust in climate scientists.

Though this may seem surprising in our polarized context, Americans share many values and beliefs.

Sources:

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2023/08/09/why-some-americans-do-not-see-urgency-on-climate-change/ 

https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/01/15/americans-confidence-in-scientists/

trust_competence_1: How incompetent or competent are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very incompetent to 100: very competent

trust_competence_3: How unqualified or qualified are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very unqualified to 100: very qualified
trust_integrity_1: How dishonest or honest are most climate scientists? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very dishonest to 100: very honest

trust_benevolence_3: How inconsiderate or considerate are most climate scientists of others’ interests? The person answers on a slider from 0: Very inconsiderate to 100: very considerate

concern_2: How serious a problem is climate change? The person answers on a slider from 0: Not at all to 100: Extremely

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture.

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. education: High school diploma / GED.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture.

Predict the mean answer for each question for a representative sample of 5000 people of this demographic. income: $100,000 to $167,999.
Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

Before the participants were asked these questions, they were instructed to read:

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture. 

Climate science is a collective effort to get closer to the truth, even if that means revising our ideas and results again and again.”

Prof. Douglas Maraun at the University of Graz in Austria is a climate scientist researching climate change. His research group focuses on extreme weather events such as heatwaves, heavy precipitation, droughts and storms. Here is what he says about his approach to research.

“As a climate scientist, I spend a lot of time questioning and improving my own research. I know that every mistake or unexpected result helps me understand the climate system a little better. My goal and the goal of my scientific field is not to push for a certain message of global warming, but to keep improving our understanding of how changes in regional climate might unfold in the future to provide the best possible information for decision makers.

Sometimes, new observations change what we thought we knew. For example, our climate models underestimated the observed summer warming trend in Europe. These and similar findings in other variables demonstrated that we did not correctly account for changes in air pollution. New climate research helped to improve our models such that our trend simulations have become more and more accurate over recent years. However, we still do not fully understand regional trends and require further research to draw firm conclusions.

In climate science, no one works in isolation. Our models improve when we bring together expertise from diverse fields such as atmospheric physics, chemistry and ecology. For instance, together, climate scientists and ecologists could demonstrate that the strength of a summer drought does not only depend on meteorological variables such as rainfall and temperature, but also on how the growing vegetation consumes and evaporates soil moisture.
